title: Slice-based hybrid scheduler: kernel-aware continuous batching (draft)
content:
Purpose and quick summary:
This note proposes a new continuous batching scheduler approach I'm calling the "slice-based hybrid scheduler". It sits between purely token-level coalescing and request-level batching and explicitly reasons about kernel selection and KV-cache locality when assembling slices. The goal is to improve tail latency for short requests, maintain throughput for long-running streams, reduce unfairness where bursty small requests block larger ones (and vice versa), and expose simple knobs for SLOs and cost tradeoffs.

Why a new approach (motivation):
- Token-level coalescing gives excellent throughput but can starve high-priority or short requests because it tends to favor big aggregated windows.
- Request-level batching preserves request boundaries but wastes kernel occupancy and increases per-token overhead on many small requests.
- We have additional signals available today: kernel performance profiles (latency curves for sequence-length x on GPU type y), KV-cache hit hotness per model shard, and request-level priorities/aging. A scheduler that combines these signals can better optimize for combined SLOs and economics.

High-level idea:
1) Break incoming work into small fixed-size "slices" (grouping of tokens, e.g., 8-32 tokens) rather than individual tokens or entire requests. A single request may map to multiple slices, preserving ordering via slice numbering.
2) Maintain multiple slice queues indexed by (model_variant, kernel_profile_bucket, kv_hotness_bucket, priority_bucket). These are lightweight bins that bias coalescing toward compatible work for execution.
3) Scheduler repeatedly forms batches by pulling from a small number of compatible bins to reach target GPU occupancy while respecting per-request ordering and fair-share constraints.
4) Use a scoring function that balances latency sensitivity (short-request-first), cost-efficiency (pack long homogeneous slices together), and KV-cache reuse (co-locate slices that are likely to hit the same key-shards).

Key components (details):
- Slice definition: A slice is a fixed token-length chunk with attributes: request_id, slice_id, model_id, encoding (fp16/int8), seq_len, kernel_hint (e.g., "matmul-optimized", "vmap-friendly"), kv_keys_hash (compact), priority.
- Binning: On enqueue, we compute kernel_hint and kv_hotness_shard (hash of KV keys modulo N) heuristics and assign the slice to a bin key = (model_variant, kernel_hint_bucket, kv_shard_bucket, priority_bucket). We keep small per-bin queues to limit scanning costs.
- Scoring function: For each candidate batch, score = w_latency * latency_gain_estimate + w_throughput * throughput_gain_estimate + w_cache * kv_affinity_score - w_fairness * fairness_penalty. These components are estimated from lightweight tables updated from telemetry (recent kernel run profiles, cache hit stats, and observed wait times).
- Fairness/aging: Each request has an age counter (time since first slice arrival). Fairness_penalty increases with age to prevent starvation. We also keep soft windows per tenant/route so a single tenant cannot fill the GPU for long.
- Ordering: Within a request we preserve ordering by ensuring slice N is not executed before slice N-1. We allow limited out-of-order execution across independent requests.

Kernel-aware placement:
- We mark slices with a kernel_hint at enqueue time based on the expected sequence length and encoder/decoder mix. The scheduler preferentially groups slices with the same kernel_hint so that the runtime can pick optimal kernels and launch fewer customized kernels per batch.
- When kernels differ, the scheduler may still coalesce slices into a batch but will annotate the batch with a "mixed-kernel" flag that triggers the runtime to dispatch per-slice kernel selection (falling back to a conservative kernel if that yields fewer kernel launches overall). We bias against mixed-kernel batches unless occupancy gain is significant.

KV-cache affinity:
- KV usage often benefits from spatial locality (same prompt prefixes or user sessions). We compute a compact KV fingerprint per slice (xxhash over recent tokens / session id) and bin on kv_shard_bucket. Co-locating slices from the same shard increases KV-hit rate and reduces memory movement and reload time.
- We prioritize co-location if expected KV benefit > threshold T_kv (learned from telemetry).

Handling different request shapes: streaming vs single-shot
- For streaming (chat) requests we treat new tokens as new slices arriving over time; we keep a per-stream window to avoid accumulating too many pending slices for a single stream.
- For single-shot long sequences we slice up front; the scheduler prefers to schedule contiguous slices back-to-back for cache reuse but will allow interleaving if shorter latency-sensitive slices are waiting.

Fairness model and parameters:
- Default: weighted fair queuing across routes with per-route weight from quota and SLAs.
- Age boost: linear factor after wait > 50ms, stronger after > 200ms.
- Burst damping: cap on number of slices from same request in a single batch (configurable, default 4) to avoid monopolization.
- Preemption: allow a small fraction of batch slots reserved for high-priority/low-latency slices (e.g., 10%).

Pseudocode (simplified):
- OnSliceEnqueue(slice):
    compute kernel_hint, kv_bucket, priority_bucket
    bin_key = (model_variant, kernel_hint, kv_bucket, priority_bucket)
    push slice into bin[bin_key] with timestamp
- SchedulerLoop():
    while gpu_idle_slots > 0:
      candidates = sample_top_bins(k=10)
      best_batch = null; best_score = -inf
      for combo in small_combinations(candidates):
         batch = form_batch(combo, target_tokens)
         if respects_ordering(batch) and respects_burst_caps(batch):
            score = score_batch(batch)
            if score > best_score: best = batch; best_score = score
      if best_batch: dispatch(best_batch) else: wait_short_and_retry()

Metrics to track (minimum):
- P50/P90/P99 latency per route and per request-length bucket (including serialization at slice boundaries)
- Throughput (tokens/sec) per GPU type and model_variant
- KV-cache hit rate per shard and change in effective memory bandwidth
- Kernel launch counts per batch and average kernel latency
- Fairness: tail wait-time distribution per route/tenant and fraction of batches with a single-tenant dominance
- Scheduling overhead CPU cycles and decision latency

Rollout plan and experiments:
1) Simulation: run offline simulator using production trace (sampled) to estimate delta in P95 and throughput compared to token-level coalescer and request-level batching.
2) Shadow mode: run scheduler in parallel in prod serving plane but do not control dispatch; compare decisions to current scheduler and compute expected impacts.
3) Canary: enable on small fleet with forced conservative knobs (high age boost, low mixed-kernel tolerance).
4) Gradual ramp with telemetry checks: KV-hit, kernel-launch inflation, fairness regressions.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve in follow-ups:
- Slice size tuning: fixed vs adaptive slice sizing (should slice size vary with request-length/priority?). I expect adaptive slices based on per-request remaining length will help but increases complexity.
- Cost of bin explosion: tradeoff between fine-grained bins (better locality) and higher scanning/metadata cost. We need an LRU eviction policy for rarely used bins.
- Multi-model batches: for small requests hitting different model variants, is it ever worthwhile to co-batch across models if kernels are compatible? Provisional answer: only if kernel_hint and encoding match and KV affinity is irrelevant.
- Runtime interface and contract: need a small API for scheduler -> runtime to express mixed-kernel batches, per-slice kernel hints, and KV-shard hints. Proposal below.

Runtime contract (minimal):
- dispatch_batch(batch_id, slice_list, batch_meta) where batch_meta includes: model_variant, kernel_mode_hint, mixed_kernel_flag, kv_shard_map, ordering_constraints
- runtime may reject batch with reason "kernel_conflict" or "kv_state_invalid" and scheduler should have a fast fallback path (e.g., break into smaller batches).

Backward compatibility and fallbacks:
- Scheduler should be feature-flagged and support a compatibility mode where kernel_hint is ignored and kv_bucket=all. This makes behavior closer to token-level coalescing for early rollout.

Instrumented experiments I propose we run in the simulator/shadow runs:
- Compare pure token-coalesce, request-batch, and slice-hybrid on: P99 latency of 1–8 token requests, throughput for 1k-token streams, KV-hit delta, and kernel-launchs per 10k tokens.
- Ablation: disable kv-affinity to quantify its impact.
- Kernel-sensitivity: run different kernel_hint bucketing granularity (2 buckets vs 5 buckets) to measure runtime kernel-launch cost vs scheduling benefit.

Operational knobs we should expose in Console:
- target_slice_size (8-64 tokens), per-route fair_weight, age_boost_ms thresholds, mixed_kernel_threshold, kv_affinity_weight, per-tenant burst_cap.

Security and multi-tenant considerations:
- KV-fingerprint must be a compact irreversibly-hashed value (no plaintext session ids) to avoid leaking identifiers into scheduling telemetry.
- Per-tenant caps are enforced in scheduler before batch formation to prevent noisy neighbors.

Appendix: quick examples
- Example A (chatty web UI): many small (1–4 token) requests from many users. Slice-hybrid will form small slices (8 tokens) and prefer mixed-source batches where kernel_hint matches; age boost will ensure single-user streams don’t hold all slots.
- Example B (long generation batch job): 2k-token single-shot requests sliced into 32-token slices; scheduler tries to schedule contiguous slices back-to-back for cache reuse unless a latency-sensitive short request arrives.

Next steps (near-term):
- Implement offline simulator + replay from 2 weeks of traces. Owner: Jordan Park. Target: simulation results by 2025-02-18.
- Define minimal runtime API for mixed-kernel and kv-hints. Owner: Michael Chen (runtime). Target: 2025-02-10.
- Shadow runs (small fraction): schedule after simulator shows expected gains.

Notes and references:
- Related internal tickets: SERVER-7892 (coalescer profiling), SERVER-8021 (kv hotness telemetry), PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/412 (kernel profiling hooks).
- This doc intentionally focuses on scheduler-level policies; detailed microbench kernel changes belong in runtime docs.

Questions I want feedback on:
- Is slice size 8–32 tokens a reasonable starting point for our two most common GPU types?
- Acceptable default for mixed_kernel_threshold (how much occupancy gain justifies extra kernel launches)?
- Any obvious security concerns with KV fingerprinting approach?
